messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At forty-nine, Marco had spent two decades building a name for himself in New York’s fashion industry, known for his meticulous attention to detail and his ability to envision a collection months, sometimes years, in advance. That capacity for forward thinking had collapsed entirely in the fourteen months since his wife, Elena, had been struck by a delivery truck while crossing Seventh Avenue. He had not been there. He had been in a fitting room, approving a hemline, when the call came. By the time he reached the hospital, she was already in surgery. The neurosurgeon’s words — “she may not wake up” — had landed somewhere in his chest and never left. She had woken, eventually, but the recovery had been slow, and Marco had stopped making plans of any kind. When a buyer asked about his fall line, he said he was “taking a season off.” When his studio manager mentioned a trunk show in March, Marco felt his throat close. He could not bring himself to agree to anything that sat beyond the immediate hour. The future had become a place where terrible things happened without warning, and he refused to walk into it willingly.

The memory of that day arrived in fragments, and the fragments were unbearable. He could see the pattern of the hospital floor tiles with excruciating clarity — little speckled squares of beige and brown — but the face of the nurse who had led him to the waiting room was a complete blank. He remembered the smell of antiseptic and the sound of a vending machine humming, but he could not recall whether he had sat down or remained standing. These gaps terrified him. He would be standing in his kitchen, reaching for a coffee cup, and suddenly he was back in that hallway, his knees weak, his stomach dropping, and the emotion would hit him so hard that he had to grip the counter and breathe slowly until it passed. What came with the memory, every time, was guilt. He had been approving a hemline. He had been thinking about fabric swatches while a truck was bearing down on his wife. The guilt was not a thought he could argue with; it was a physical sensation, a weight in his ribs, and it made him want to disappear.

He tried not to think about any of it. He kept his mind occupied constantly. When he was not at the hospital sitting beside Elena’s bed, he was in his home studio, sorting buttons by size, reorganizing his thread cabinet, sketching designs he knew he would never produce. He listened to podcasts while he worked — true crime, history, anything with a narrative that demanded his attention. Silence was dangerous. In silence, the images came. At night, sleep was nearly impossible. He lay beside Elena, who was home now but still fragile, and listened to her breathing. Every time she shifted, his heart hammered. He was certain, in those dark hours, that something was about to go wrong again. He had not told her this. She thought he was just restless.

The triggers were everywhere, and they were physical. A delivery truck rumbling past his window made his hands shake. The squeal of brakes outside a coffee shop sent a bolt of heat through his chest, and he would have to set down his cup before he dropped it. He had stopped walking anywhere near Seventh Avenue. He took the long way to the subway, adding twenty minutes to his commute, and he had begun to avoid the neighborhood where the accident happened entirely. His assistant had noticed. She had asked, gently, if he wanted her to handle the meetings with the fabric suppliers who were based in that part of town. He had said yes, and he had felt a wave of relief so deep it shamed him.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of quiet. Elena had asked him, over dinner, if he wanted to visit her sister in California next summer. She had said it casually, as if the future were still a place one could discuss. Marco had opened his mouth to answer and found that he could not. The word “yes” would not come. The word “no” felt like a betrayal. He had sat there, silent, until Elena put down her fork and looked at him with an expression he recognized as worry. He was afraid, he realized, of everything. He was afraid of planning, afraid of sleeping, afraid of the gaps in his own memory, and most of all, he was afraid of the guilt that sat inside him like a second skeleton. He did not know if therapy could help, but he knew he could not go on like this — a man who had once designed entire seasons, now unable to say yes to a summer trip.
